lines: Mason jokes are solid. Sometimes too solid to move.
I tried a lighter mason joke once. It still landed like a brick.
My best jokes have foundations. The punchline usually needs <jump>scaffolding</jump>.
I told a joke at the stonecutter once. The workstation took it better than the villagers did.
People say I work too much. I say the work is the only one here that listens.
If confidence could be traded, this village would be rich and still somehow underprepared.
I tried taking a day off. The village immediately treated it like an emergency drill.
A good joke needs timing. Around here, timing usually trips over a chicken.
I would laugh louder, but someone would ask me to explain it and ruin everything.
The bell has one joke. It screams, and everyone suddenly remembers they have legs.
Mason jokes are solid, if a little dense.
I had a stone joke, but it weighed on people.
A brick joke needs careful setup.
My arch joke only works under pressure.
I told a mortar joke and it held the room together.
A chisel joke makes a fine point slowly.
The wall laughed once, but it was mostly settling.
I know a foundation joke, but it takes time to appreciate.
A stair joke has too many steps.
My gravel joke fell apart immediately.
The stonecutter has a cutting sense of humor.
I tried a polished joke. Too smooth to grip.
A doorway joke works best if it has an opening.
The roof heard my joke and said I was beneath it.
I asked the block for feedback. It was stone silent.
